page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: Enthalpy H is the total heat content of a
system at constant pressure. It is defined
It is a state function and an extensive
steps.why: H bundles the internal energy with the pV term so that one quantity tracks the heat exchanged when the pressure, not the volume, is held constant. The board wording total heat content is loose and must not be read as H = q: H is a state function while heat is a path function, so the only link to heat is that the CHANGE in H equals the heat exchanged at constant pressure, qp = ΔH.
common_mistakes: Writing H = U − pV. The pV term is added.
Calling H a path function — like U, it is a state function.
steps.memory_tip: H is U plus the pV term: the internal energy plus the product of pressure and volume, which is itself an energy.
steps.margin_note: The equation H = U + pV must appear.

steps.label: Why it is useful
lines: At constant pressure the heat absorbed by
the system equals its enthalpy change:
Most reactions run in open vessels at
constant pressure, so ΔH is the heat

lines.text: H = U + pV;  qp = ΔH at constant pressure

steps.why: The definition is chosen exactly so that the measurable heat of an open-vessel reaction is a state-function change — that is the reason chemistry works with ΔH rather than ΔU.
common_mistakes: Writing qv = ΔH — heat at constant volume measures ΔU; heat at constant pressure measures ΔH.
steps.memory_tip: Open vessel, constant pressure, heat = ΔH. Sealed vessel, constant volume, heat = ΔU.
steps.margin_note: The qp = ΔH line is what makes the definition useful.

insider_note: Half of this question is never asked out loud: the second mark is why enthalpy is worth defining at all, qp = ΔH. A textbook-perfect definition with H = U + pV and nothing after it scores one.
